title: The hypertrophy series: handling lower body volume & intensity
summary: Pointers for programming lower body work for sustainable tonnage progression without injury. NH trains legs every two days, alternating heavy and lighter days, keeps heavy squat/deadlift days short, and gives his preferred rep windows for deadlifts and squats.
claims: Specialization like Smolov costs the rest of the program and then leaves a tonnage drop once it ends, so he always promotes stability
Leg training taxes the lower back heavily because the best leg hypertrophy lifts rely on it
Perfect form on every rep is essential; mechanical failure means you did something wrong
Even with perfect form, poor volume and intensity management causes overuse injury
One leg day a week is terrible advice for naturals, but training legs hard every day also doesn't work
He trains legs every two days, alternating heavy squat/deadlift days with lighter, higher-rep variations
Not every leg session must be excruciating; treat legs like biceps with some lighter, higher-rep work
High reps for legs are a requirement; poor cardio is a weak point to address
Leg days shouldn't be three hours: heavy compounds give lots of tonnage quickly, so heavy squat/deadlift days should be the shortest
When muscular endurance is shot, stop and go home; pushing baby weight does nothing
He deadlifts conventional in a 2-5 rep window because he can always tell if his form is off
He never squats for 2 reps; his squat window is 4-8 with a minimum of 4
Very high reps on squats and deadlifts end in cardiovascular or mechanical failure, not muscular failure, and risk injury
Use lifts that can't fail mechanically for high-volume leg work: Romanian deadlifts, pause squats, box squats
